schema.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a proposal you made with start_session (initiation "own_initiative" or "offer") that the user has not started.

Call this when it went stale: the work was done here after all (by you or the user), it turned out unnecessary, or you proposed a better-scoped replacement (propose the new one first, then dismiss the old task_id). A card the user answered has already left, "Do it here" included, so it needs no call.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__hand_off_to_session
tools.description: Move the task you are in the middle of into its own session (a fork of this conversation plus your remaining plan) so you can answer the user now. Use it when a new user message about something else arrives mid-task — not for small corrections or when the user said to keep the work here. In a worktree the fork gets a fresh worktree, normally cut from your branch tip: commit first (uncommitted edits stay here). Bold title line and one sentence right before the call; after it, stop that task here and answer the new message — no recap.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

scope.description: Required with items: "first_task", "continuation" or "new_task" (see the tool description). Omit on advance / done / start updates.

session.description: When you delegated this step to a session you started: that session's short name (from start_session's result). The app shows its live state on the step.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields (write recap last) — ask and recap are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Like the recap, never point at anything else in the conversation. Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available, or one your own work this turn made available; others are refused, and one that later stops being available is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and other answers), so do not guess. Offer commit, create_pr or verify only once the work the user asked for is done, not every turn. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Not now": a button, not a sentence. A click sends it to you as the user's answer. Never a go-ahead to commit: that is the commit app action. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments. Never repeat an offer the user passed over, as an app action, a reply or a question in your closing message, unless what it acts on has changed since or they bring it up.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

action.description:

* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control
tools.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control
schema.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'press_key' presses a hardware key 'count' times: return, delete (backspace), an arrow, select_all, undo or redo (a key also hides the on-screen keyboard); 'set_appearance' switches the device to light or dark mode; 'appearance' says which it is in; 'set_keyboard' shows or hides the on-screen keyboard (it appears only while a text field has focus, and 'press_key' and 'text' hide it again); 'rotate' turns the device a quarter turn left or right ('direction'); take a 'screenshot' after it and tap in that screenshot's frame, however it comes back; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). Start more than 4pt from the edge to drag or scroll content near the bezel.

app_path.description: For 'launch': absolute path (no ~) to the built .app bundle (e.g. /Users/me/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData/MyApp-abc123/Build/Products/Debug-iphonesimulator/MyApp.app).

device.description: Simulator name (e.g. 'iPhone 17 Pro') or UDID. Defaults to the simulator already attached, else the first booted one. The first use of a device asks the user for permission.

udid.description: Alias for 'device' (identical semantics: simulator name or UDID). Pass at most one of 'device' / 'udid'.

bundle_id.description: For 'launch': bundle identifier. If omitted, extracted from the .app's Info.plist.

points.description: For 'touch_path': touch path samples in device points. First point is touch-down; last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000 ms; the first sample's is skipped, so send 0 or omit it; at most 30 seconds in all).

points2.description: For 'touch2_path': two-finger path samples in device points. Each sample carries both contacts (x1/y1, x2/y2); first is touch-down, last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000 ms; the first sample's is skipped, so send 0 or omit it; at most 30 seconds in all).

duration.description: Seconds. For 'tap', >0.5 is a long-press. For 'swipe', the gesture duration (default 0.3).

key.description: For 'press_key': the key or edit command to press.

count.description: For 'press_key': how many times to press it, 1 to 20 (default 1).

state.description: For 'set_keyboard': 'show' or 'hide' the on-screen keyboard. For 'set_appearance': 'light' or 'dark'.

url.description: For 'open_url': URL or scheme to open in the simulator.

Show visual content — SVG graphics, diagrams, charts, or interactive HTML widgets — that renders inline alongside your text response.
Use for flowcharts, architecture diagrams, dashboards, forms, calculators, data tables, games, illustrations, or any visual content.
The code is auto-detected: starts with <svg = SVG mode, otherwise HTML mode.
A global sendPrompt(text) function is available — it sends a message to chat as if the user typed it.
IMPORTANT: Call read_me before your first show_widget call. Do NOT narrate or mention the read_me call to the user — call it silently, then respond as if you went straight to building the visualization.

loading_messages.description: 1–4 loading messages shown to the user while the visual renders, each roughly 5 words long. Write them in the same language the user is using. Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. Playful examples — revenue chart: ['Bribing bars to stand taller', 'Asking Q4 where it went']; kanban: ['Herding cards into columns', 'Dragging, dropping, not stopping'].

title.description: Short snake_case identifier for this visual. Must be specific and disambiguating — if the conversation has multiple visuals, this title alone should tell you which one is being referenced (e.g. 'q4_revenue_by_product_line' not 'chart', 'oauth_login_flow' not 'diagram'). Also used as the download filename, so no spaces or special characters.

widget_code.description: SVG or HTML code to render. For SVG: raw SVG code starting with <svg> tag, must use CSS variables for colors. Example: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">...</svg>. For HTML: raw HTML content to render, do NOT include DOCTYPE, <html>, <head>, or <body> tags. Use CSS variables for theming. Keep background transparent and avoid top-level padding. Scripts are supported but execute after streaming completes.

attachment.cliPrefix: You are Claude Code, Anthropic's official CLI for Claude, running within the Claude Agent SDK.

definition.name: mcp__claude-artifacts__edit_version
definition.description: Publish a new version of an artifact you own, or of one in your organization that you can edit (some clients refuse any artifact but your own as owner-only), by replacing text in its current document: use it for a small change instead of sending the whole page to publish_version. The server reads the live index.html, applies every edit in order, and publishes the result as one new version; if any edit cannot be applied, nothing is published. Each old_text must occur exactly once in the document as it stands when that edit is applied: include enough surrounding text to make it unique. base_version must name the live version (from get_artifact, read_artifact, list_files or your last publish result); if it is no longer live the call is rejected with a conflict that names the live version: read what you are changing again and retry. To rename the artifact pass title, which also rewrites the document's <title> element; an edit to that element without title is refused, because the server keeps it in step with the artifact's title. Artifacts that contain a live (collaboratively edited) document cannot be edited here. An artifact made from a type is edited only if this server offers list_files, and only with path: one of its own text files, as list_files lists them, never its page or its type's files.

artifact_title.description: The artifact's current title, as get_artifact gives it. Needed when shared_live is 'public'.

base_version.description: The version id these edits apply to: the live version, as get_artifact, read_artifact, list_files or your last publish result returned it.

## claude-artifacts
Claude may publish its own work without being asked, because artifacts start private. The exception is content that could mislead or cause harm if shared further: anything that imitates a real organization, person or record, and anything the person presented as sensitive. Claude builds those as files and lets the person decide whether they get a URL. content.text:
**Yes, 6 and 7 are valid time signatures, but they never appear in your source data.** Your cleaning code isn't removing them.

| Value | `kaggle_114k_songs.csv` | `kaggle_1m_songs.csv` | Your cleaning |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| 0 | 163 | 1,228 | set to NaN |
| 1 | 973 | 12,660 | set to NaN |
| 3 | 9,195 | 112,332 | kept |
| 4 | 101,843 | 1,010,673 | kept |
| 5 | 1,826 | 22,871 | kept |
| 6 | 0 | 0 | n/a |
| 7 | 0 | 0 | n/a |

[pull_all.py:225](spotifysongs/pull_all.py:225) keeps anything from 3 to 7, so it would have kept 6 and 7 if they were there.

**Are they valid?** Musically, yes. Spotify's API docs describe this field as an estimate ranging from 3 to 7, meaning 3/4 through 7/4, and that's probably where your 3–7 range came from. 6/4 and 7/4 both exist in real music, such as the 7/4 sections of Pink Floyd's "Money".

**Why are they missing?** The most likely reason is that Spotify's estimator doesn't output 6 or 7 in practice, even though the docs allow them. That's my inference, since I can't see how Spotify's model works. It fits the data, though: both files have exactly the same five values, even with about 1.16 million songs in the larger one. Songs in 7/4 certainly exist in a catalog that size, so they were probably labeled as something else.

It also means the column doesn't tell you a song's true meter. For example, a 7/4 song may be labeled 3, 4 or 5, and the 0 and 1 values you drop look like failed or unreliable estimates.

**For your package:** `time_signature_6` and `time_signature_7` exist in `spotify_songs.parquet`, but they're zero for all 35,882 rows.
- **Modeling:** these columns can't help a model, so drop them before fitting. In a linear model they just add useless features, and anything that divides by a column's standard deviation will divide by zero.
- **Documentation:** your README lists these columns, so add a note that they're always empty in this data. Otherwise, people may assume those songs exist.

content.text:
**No, only `time_signature_6` and `time_signature_7` are useless, because they're all zeros.** The 3, 4 and 5 columns could still help, but I'd expect a weak signal at best. I haven't tested this against your target.

- **Little variation:** about 89.6% of your songs are labeled 4, 8.5% are labeled 3 and 1.9% are labeled 5. A feature that's the same for 9 out of 10 songs can't separate most of them, though it could still matter for the other 10%.
- **Noisy labels:** these are Spotify's estimates, not true meters, so some songs are probably mislabeled. That tends to weaken any real relationship.
- **Overlap with other features:** time signature may partly track genre, such as more 3/4 in some folk or country music. If so, your genre columns may already capture some of the same information.

**Before fitting:**
1. Drop `time_signature_6` and `time_signature_7`.
2. For linear or logistic regression, also drop one of the remaining three, ideally `time_signature_4` so it serves as the baseline. Every row has exactly one of them set to 1 (3,050 + 32,143 + 689 = 35,882), so together they duplicate the intercept. Tree-based models don't need this step.

You could also combine them into a single `is_4_4` column, which is simpler but loses the difference between 3 and 5.

**To find out if it helps:** compare cross-validated scores with and without these columns, using the same folds. If the score doesn't improve beyond the normal variation between folds, drop them and keep the simpler model. That result would only apply to your target and model, so a different target could still benefit.

content.text:
**You can collapse genre into 10 columns, and samba fits fine, but if you're predicting popularity, grouping by musical similarity throws away most of the signal.** I assumed popularity is your target, based on your earlier homework, so these results may not apply to a different one.

| Genre columns (ridge regression, genre only) | 5-fold CV R² |
|---|---:|
| All 113 genres | 0.639 |
| 10 groups based on popularity | 0.612 |
| 10 musical groups | 0.162 |

**Why the musical groups do so badly:** genres that sound alike can have very different popularity, and collapsing them averages that away. Your own example shows this, since `alt-rock` and `k-pop` would be merged into groups with very different genres:
- **Pop group:** `power-pop` averages 26.6, while `pop` averages 75.3.
- **Rock group:** `goth` averages 30.5, while `rock` averages 73.1.
- **Electronic group:** `detroit-techno` averages 11.0, while `dance` averages 77.7.

**What I'd do**
- **To predict popularity:** keep all 113 columns with a regularized or tree-based model. If you need 10 or fewer, use the popularity-based bins, which sort genres into 10 groups by average popularity. Learn the bins from the training data only, inside each fold, or you'll leak the target. The groups won't mean anything musically.
- **To explain or plot results:** use the musical groups below, because they're easy to interpret.

Either way, remove `genre_songwriter` or `genre_singer-songwriter`, because the two columns are identical.

**Musical mapping:** this covers all 113 genres, and samba goes in `latin_brazil` with `pagode`, `mpb`, `forro` and `sertanejo`.

| Group | Songs | Genres |
|---|---:|---|
| `electronic` | 9,716 | edm, electronic, electro, house, deep-house, chicago-house, progressive-house, techno, detroit-techno, minimal-techno, trance, dubstep, drum-and-bass, breakbeat, hardstyle, idm, trip-hop, club, dance, j-dance, party |
| `rock` | 4,727 | rock, alt-rock, alternative, indie, hard-rock, psych-rock, rock-n-roll, rockabilly, j-rock, grunge, punk, punk-rock, emo, goth, ska, garage, guitar |
| `world` | 4,102 | indian, afrobeat, dancehall, reggae, dub, world-music, french, german, swedish, turkish, malay, british |
| `metal` | 3,952 | metal, heavy-metal, death-metal, black-metal, metalcore, grindcore, hardcore, industrial |
| `latin_brazil` | 3,714 | latin, latino, salsa, samba, tango, reggaeton, forro, sertanejo, pagode, mpb, brazil, spanish |
| `other` | 3,582 | comedy, kids, children, disney, show-tunes, anime, sad, happy, romance |
| `pop` | 3,315 | pop, indie-pop, power-pop, synth-pop, k-pop, j-pop, j-idol, cantopop, mandopop, pop-film |
| `classical_ambient` | 3,171 | classical, opera, piano, ambient, new-age, sleep, study, chill |
| `hiphop_soul_jazz` | 2,076 | hip-hop, r-n-b, soul, funk, groove, gospel, disco, blues, jazz |
| `folk_country` | 1,908 | country, bluegrass, honky-tonk, folk, acoustic, songwriter, singer-songwriter |

Songs can have several genres, so set a group to 1 if any of its genres is 1 (use `max`, not `sum`). About 11% of songs land in more than one group, so the counts add up to more than your 35,882 rows.

**Things to watch out for**
- **Judgment calls:** some placements are debatable, such as `garage`, `ska`, `dub` and `disco`. Labels like `sad`, `happy` and `british` describe a mood or a place rather than a sound.
- **Results may look too good:** an R² of 0.639 from genre alone is surprisingly high, and popularity within a genre can be very tight (samba's SD is 4.3, compared with 18.4 overall). That may reflect how the Kaggle authors collected songs for each genre rather than anything about the music. If so, the model may not do as well on songs collected another way.
- **Audio features not included:** these scores use genre only, so the gap between groupings could shrink once you add features like `energy` or `loudness`. Rerun the comparison on your full feature set before deciding.

message.content: new question. I want to use time signature as a categroical feature. If I wanted to add another categroical feature that had multiple classes like key, does each feature need its own OneHotEncoder, or can they share?

content.text:
**They can share.** A single `OneHotEncoder` can handle several columns at once: it learns each column's categories separately and creates a separate set of output columns for each one.

```python
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder

cat_cols = ["time_signature", "key"]

encoder = OneHotEncoder(sparse_output=False, handle_unknown="ignore")
encoded = encoder.fit_transform(train_df[cat_cols])

encoder.categories_               # one array of categories per column
encoder.get_feature_names_out()   # time_signature_3, ..., key_0, ..., key_11
```

Fit it on the training data only, then call `encoder.transform(test_df[cat_cols])` on the test data, so both sets get the same columns.

If you're using a model pipeline, `ColumnTransformer` encodes the categorical columns and leaves the rest as they are:

```python
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer

preprocess = ColumnTransformer(
    [("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), cat_cols)],
    remainder="passthrough",
)
```

You'd only need separate encoders if the columns need different settings, such as dropping a baseline category for one but not the other. In that case, give each one its own entry in the `ColumnTransformer`.

**In your data:** `spotify_songs.parquet` already has `key_0`–`key_11` and `time_signature_3`–`time_signature_7`, but not the original `key` or `time_signature` columns. If you're loading that file, these features are already encoded, so you don't need an encoder. You can just select those columns, leaving out the all-zero `time_signature_6` and `time_signature_7`.

For linear or logistic regression, also drop one column from each set (for example, `time_signature_4` and `key_0`), since each set adds up to 1 in every row and duplicates the intercept. If you do use the encoder on raw data, `drop="first"` does this, but it drops the first category in each column (3 and 0) rather than letting you choose a baseline like `time_signature_4`.

message.content: if all I'm doing is displaying decision boundaries for an assignment, that means it's okay to use all of the data right? No need for a train-test split. Do not give me code. I just want guidance like you're a professor and I'm a student

content.text:
Mostly yes. If the goal is to show what shape of boundary a model draws, fitting on all the data is reasonable. You aren't claiming anything about how well the model generalizes, and that's the question a train-test split exists to answer. Check the assignment wording first, though, because if it asks for test performance or says to plot on held-out data, that takes priority.

The line you need to watch is what you claim from the plot. A boundary fit on all the data shows what the model learned from those points, and that's all. If you can say "here is how this model carves up the feature space," you're fine. If you find yourself saying "this model works well" or "this one is better," you've made a claim about generalization that the plot can't support.

This matters most when you compare models. Take a very flexible model, like a deep decision tree or k-NN with k=1. It can wrap itself around every training point and look like it's classifying beautifully, when it may just be overfitting. So a jagged boundary with few visible mistakes isn't evidence of a good model. In fact, spotting that is often the point of the exercise.

As you write this up, ask yourself:

1. **What does the assignment want me to conclude?** If it's about how settings like tree depth or k change the boundary's shape, you don't need a split. If it asks which setting is best, you do.
2. **Am I reporting a number next to the plot?** An accuracy computed on the same data you fit is training accuracy. You can report it, but label it that way.
3. **Would I describe this plot differently if I had new data on it?** Try imagining new points scattered across it. Where would the boundary look confident but probably be wrong? That's a good thing to discuss in your interpretation.

State your choice openly, too. One sentence is enough: "I fit on the full dataset because these plots illustrate model behavior, not predictive performance." That tells your grader you understood the distinction, rather than just forgetting to split.

"""

from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier

###################################################################################

    {

]

###################################################################################
# FUNCTIONS
###################################################################################

def build_pipeline(num: list, cat: list) -> Pipeline:
    """
    Build a pipeline given the numerical and categorical features.

    Parameters:
        num (list): numeric feature names.
        cat (list): categorical feature names.

    Returns:
        Pipeline.
    """

    # Create feature transformers
    transformers = []
    if num:
        transformers.append(("num", StandardScaler(), num))
    if cat:
        transformers.append(("cat", OneHotEncoder(sparse_output=False,
                                                  handle_unknown="ignore",
                                                  drop="first"),
                                                  cat,
                                                  ))

    # Return pipeline
    return Pipeline([
        ("prep", ColumnTransformer(transformers)),
        ("knn", KNeighborsClassifier(fit_intercept=True,   # add col of 1's
                                     n_neighbors=10,
                                     random_state=SEED,    # set seed
                                     )),
    ])

def evaluate_cross_validation(model_schema: dict,
                              target: pd.Series,
                              train: pd.DataFrame,
                              ) -> dict:
    """
    Evaluate logistic regression of a model.

    Parameters:
        model_schema (dict): schema of model names and features.
        target (pd.Series): the target to predict.
        train (pd.DataFrame): the features for training.

    Returns:
        Dict. Returns model results as a dictionary.
    """

    # Create Pipeline object
    model_pipeline = build_pipeline(num=model_schema["num"],
                                    cat=model_schema["cat"],
                                    )

    # Get list of features
    features = model_schema["num"] + model_schema["cat"]

    # Do cross validation for a model
    cv_output = cross_validate(
            model_pipeline,
            train[features],
            target,
            cv=KFold(NUM_CV, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED),
            scoring=["accuracy"],
            return_estimator=True,
            )

    # Return scores
    results = {}
    for metric_name, values in cv_output.items():
        if "test_" in metric_name:
            results[metric_name] = values

    return results

###################################################################################

Your overall structure is right: one model per k, drawn on its own axis in a loop. The problems are in how the pieces connect, and one of them, feature scaling, will quietly make your plots wrong even after the errors are gone. I found these by reading [knn.py](homework4/knn.py) without running it.

## Where you're going wrong

1. **The boundary isn't going to your subplot (line 161).** You never tell `DecisionBoundaryDisplay.from_estimator` which axis to use, so each call draws on a new figure. Your three subplots would get only the scatter points. Look at its `ax` parameter.
2. **`features[:, 0]` won't work (line 173).** That's NumPy-style indexing, but `features` is a DataFrame. Select the columns by name instead.
3. **`y_train` doesn't exist (line 174).** Which variable holds your target in this script?
4. **The title line has three mistakes (line 184).**
   - `title` isn't the method that sets an Axes title.
   - `sep=` belongs to `print`, not to plot titles.
   - `i` is the loop position (0, 1, 2), not the value of k.
5. **Your features aren't scaled (line 155).** This is the most important one conceptually. kNN uses distance, tempo spans roughly a hundred or more units, and valence only spans 0 to 1. What will that do to "nearest"? You'd effectively be plotting a tempo-only model.

## Checklist

**Part 1**
- [ ] Add scaling by fitting a pipeline (scaler, then kNN) inside the loop, rather than a bare classifier.
- [ ] Set each model's k from `k_values`.
- [ ] Pass the current subplot axis to the boundary display.
- [ ] Fix the scatter's x and y values, and use your actual target for the colors.
- [ ] Set a title that shows the real k value.
- [ ] Make the points small and semi-transparent, and remove the black edges. With about 35,000 points, your current settings could hide the boundary entirely.
- [ ] Label both axes and call a layout adjustment before saving, so the subplots don't overlap.
- [ ] Run it and compare the plots. Does k=1 look jagged and k=50 look smoother? If not, go back and check your scaling.

**Before Part 2**
- [ ] Remove `fit_intercept` and `random_state` from `KNeighborsClassifier` (line 88). kNN doesn't accept either one, so `build_pipeline` will crash.
- [ ] Add a parameter for k to `build_pipeline`, since it's currently fixed at 10. You can then reuse this function in Part 1.
- [ ] Fix `NUM_CV` (line 123), because the constant you defined is `NUM_FOLDS`.
- [ ] Rethink `CAT_FEATURES = [TIME_SIGS]` (line 47). It's a list inside a list, and those columns are already one-hot encoded, so they don't need an encoder.

**One question to answer in your write-up:** which k is overfitting and which is underfitting, and how can you tell from the shape of the boundary?

message.content: if I pass already one-hot encoded columns to OneHotEncoder, what happens?

content.text:
It runs without an error, but it treats each column as its own category with two values, 0 and 1, and encodes each one again. What you get depends on your settings:

- **With `drop="first"` (your current setting):** each column's 0 category is dropped, leaving just its 1 column. You get back the same values, with new names like `time_signature_3_1`. It's redundant, but harmless.
- **Without `drop`:** each column turns into two, one for "is 0" and one for "is 1". Your column count doubles, and every pair is perfectly redundant.

There are two side effects to watch for:

- **Baselines:** `drop="first"` drops the 0 category within each column, not one whole column from the set. So you'd still have all of `time_signature_3`, `_4` and `_5`, and they'd still add up to 1 in every row. For a linear model, you'd still need to drop one yourself.
- **Empty columns:** `time_signature_6` and `_7` only ever contain 0. With `drop="first"`, that one category gets dropped, so they disappear from the output, which happens to be convenient. Without `drop`, each stays as one constant column of 1s. In both cases, a fold or test set containing an unseen value would be handled differently, though that can't happen here since these columns are always 0.

So for your homework, skip the encoder and pass those columns straight through. In a `ColumnTransformer`, you can do this with `"passthrough"` as the transformer for those columns. It also matters for kNN: every feature counts toward distance, so the doubled columns from the no-`drop` case would make time signature count twice as much.

message.content: how do I configure the onehot encoder to have anything from TIME_SIGS passthrough as is?

content.text:
You don't configure it on the encoder, because `OneHotEncoder` has no passthrough option. Instead, leave `TIME_SIGS` out of the encoder and give those columns their own entry in the `ColumnTransformer`, using the string `"passthrough"` where the transformer normally goes:

```python
transformers.append(("time_sigs", "passthrough", TIME_SIGS))
```

In `build_pipeline`, this would sit alongside your `"num"` and `"cat"` entries. Each entry is just a name, what to do, and which columns to do it to.

**What to change in [knn.py](homework4/knn.py):**
- **Line 47:** `CAT_FEATURES = [TIME_SIGS]` is a list inside a list, and it would send these columns to the encoder through your `"cat"` entry. Remove `TIME_SIGS` from it.
- **`build_pipeline`:** add a third parameter for the passthrough columns, with its own `if` block like the other two, so each schema can choose whether to include them.
- **`evaluate_cross_validation` (line 116):** `features` is built from `num + cat`, so add the new list there too. Otherwise, those columns won't be in the data passed to the pipeline, and it will raise an error.

**Two things to know for kNN:**
- **Scaling:** passthrough columns skip `StandardScaler`, so they stay as 0s and 1s while your numeric features are z-scores. Two songs with different time signatures differ by 1 in each of two columns, for a squared distance of 2, about the same as a 1.4 SD gap in tempo. Time signature can therefore have a real effect on who counts as "nearest", so it's worth checking with cross-validation whether it helps.
- **Empty columns:** `TIME_SIGS` also picks up `time_signature_6` and `_7`. Since they're always 0, they don't change any distances, so they're harmless here, but filtering them out keeps your feature list honest.

"""
Olivia Buchanan
Homework 4: kNN, Cross-validation, and PCA
"""

import spotifysongs
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Patch
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_validate, KFold, GridSearchCV
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.inspection import DecisionBoundaryDisplay

###################################################################################
# CONSTANTS
###################################################################################

# Seed
SEED = 17
np.random.seed(SEED)

# Load all tables as their own variable
globals().update(spotifysongs.load())

# Cross validation settings
NUM_FOLDS = 5

# Targets
CAT_TARGET = "mode"
NUM_TARGET = "popularity"

# Extra info for graphs
LABEL = "title"

# Numeric features
NUM_FEATURES = [
    "tempo",
    "valence",
    "speechiness",
]

# Categorical features
TIME_SIGS = [col for col in songs.columns if col.startswith("time_signature_")]
TIME_SIGS = TIME_SIGS[:3] # filter to only time sigs 3-4 since 6-7 are empty

# Models to evaluate
SCHEMAS = [
    {
        "name": "kNN_boundary",
        "num": NUM_FEATURES[:2],
        "cat": [],
    }
]

###################################################################################
# FUNCTIONS
###################################################################################

def build_pipeline(num: list,
                   cat: list,
                   passthrough: list,
                   k: int) -> Pipeline:
    """
    Build a pipeline given the numerical and categorical features.

    Parameters:
        num (list): numeric feature names.
        cat (list): categorical feature names.
        passthrough (list): features to leave as-is.
        k (int): number of neighbors.

    Returns:
        Pipeline.
    """

    # Create feature transformers
    transformers = []
    if num:
        transformers.append(("num", StandardScaler(), num))
    if cat:
        transformers.append(("cat", OneHotEncoder(sparse_output=False,
                                                  handle_unknown="ignore",
                                                  drop="first"),
                                                  cat,
                                                  ))
    transformers.append(("pass", "passthrough", passthrough))

    # Return pipeline
    return Pipeline([
        ("prep", ColumnTransformer(transformers)),
        ("knn", KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k)),
    ])

def evaluate_cross_validation(model_schema: dict,
                              target: pd.Series,
                              train: pd.DataFrame,
                              ) -> dict:
    """
    Evaluate logistic regression of a model.

    Parameters:
        model_schema (dict): schema of model names and features.
        target (pd.Series): the target to predict.
        train (pd.DataFrame): the features for training.

    Returns:
        Dict. Returns model results as a dictionary.
    """

    # Create Pipeline object
    model_pipeline = build_pipeline(num=model_schema["num"],
                                    cat=model_schema["cat"],
                                    )

    # Get list of features
    features = model_schema["num"] + model_schema["cat"]

    # Do cross validation for a model
    cv_output = cross_validate(
            model_pipeline,
            train[features],
            target,
            cv=KFold(NUM_FOLDS, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED),
            scoring=["accuracy"],
            return_estimator=True,
            )

    # Return scores
    results = {}
    for metric_name, values in cv_output.items():
        if "test_" in metric_name:
            results[metric_name] = values

    return results

###################################################################################
# PART 1: DRAW KNN DECISION REGIIONS
###################################################################################

# Split target from features
cat_target = songs[CAT_TARGET]
num_features = songs[NUM_FEATURES[:2]]

# Set 3 k-values to explore
k_values = [1, 10, 50]

# Create plot demonstrating what happens as k-value changes
fig, ax = plt.subplots(nrows=len(k_values), ncols=1, figsize=(10, 3 * len(k_values)))

# Fill plot with decision boundaries
for i in range(len(k_values)):

    # Get pipeline
    knn_pipeline = build_pipeline(num=num_features,
                                  cat=[],
                                  passthrough=[],
                                  k=k_values[i])

    # Get color map
    cmap = plt.get_cmap("viridis_r")

    # Get decision boundaries
    DecisionBoundaryDisplay.from_estimator(
        knn_pipeline,
        ax=i,
        response_method="predict",
        plot_method="contourf",
        cmap=cmap,
        vmin=0,
        vmax=1,
    )

    # Fill plot with song data
    ax[i].scatter(
        features[:, NUM_FEATURES[0]], features[:, NUM_FEATURES[1]],
        c=(target_cat == knn.classes_[1]),
        edgecolors="black",
        cmap=cmap,
    )

    # Details for the plot
    ax[i].legend(handles=[
        Patch(color=cmap(0.0), label=knn.classes_[0]),
        Patch(color=cmap(1.0), label=knn.classes_[1]),
    ])
    ax[i].title(i, "-Nearest-Neighbors", sep="")

fig.savefig("changing_k_value.png")
plt.close(fig)

# PART 2: FIND GOOD K-VALUE
###################################################################################

**Mostly, yes.** The pipeline side is correct, but `TIME_SIGS` doesn't reach the pipeline yet. This is from reading [knn.py](homework4/knn.py), not running it.

## What's right
- **`build_pipeline` (lines 64–97):** the new parameter and the `("pass", "passthrough", passthrough)` entry are correct.
- **Removing the encoder for time signature:** `TIME_SIGS` no longer goes through `OneHotEncoder`.
- **`TIME_SIGS[:3]` (line 49):** this does pick `time_signature_3`, `_4` and `_5`, since those columns come first in your data. It does depend on that column order, though.
- **`passthrough=[]` in Part 1 (line 161):** a decision boundary plot needs exactly two features, so leaving time signature out here is correct.

## What to fix
1. **`SCHEMAS` has no passthrough entry (lines 52–58).** `TIME_SIGS` is defined but never used. When you set up Part 2, any schema that should include time signature needs a `"passthrough"` key, and schemas without it should have an empty list.
2. **Line 91 has no `if` check.** Your other two entries each have one. An empty list should still work here, because `ColumnTransformer` skips empty column selections, but adding the check keeps it consistent.
3. **The comment on line 49 is slightly off.** It says "3-4", but the columns are 3–5.

## Your next error: line 159
`num=num_features` passes a DataFrame, but `build_pipeline` expects a list of column names. `if num:` will crash on a DataFrame because its truth value is ambiguous. Pass the names instead, which you already have as `NUM_FEATURES[:2]`.

## Other Part 1 issues
These don't involve passthrough, but they'll stop Part 1 from running:
- **Lines 159–162:** the pipeline is never fit, and it has to be fit before you can plot it.
- **Lines 168–170:** `from_estimator` is missing its data argument, and `ax=i` passes the loop position instead of the subplot.
- **Lines 180–181:** `features`, `target_cat` and `knn` no longer exist under those names, and `[:, name]` still isn't valid DataFrame indexing.
- **Lines 181, 188 and 189:** once you've fit the pipeline, you can get `classes_` from it directly.
- **Line 191:** the title line is still unchanged from the issue we discussed earlier.

content.text:
**Code:** Part 1 looks correct from reading it, and you've clearly got it running. There are just two small things:
- **Line 192:** the title has an underscore in `Nearest_Neighbors`, which should be a hyphen.
- **Lines 184–189:** you lowered the opacity, but the points are still the default size. If they cover the boundary, make them smaller.

**Your question:** you're right. The plot shows what the model would predict, not how often it's correct. It helps you form a hypothesis, but it can't confirm one.

**Where the plot does help:**
- It shows how k changes the model's behavior.
- It can show whether predictions depend on the features at all. If a high-k plot is nearly one color, that hints the features aren't adding much beyond predicting the most common class. It's a clue, not proof.

**Which metrics to use:**
- **Cross-validated accuracy, compared with a baseline:** this should be your main check. If major is the more common class, always guessing major already scores well, so ask whether kNN beats that. Accuracy alone can look good while the model learns nothing.
- **Cross-validated log loss:** this is a useful addition because it rewards well-calibrated probabilities, not just correct labels. Compare it with a baseline too, such as predicting each class's overall share for every song.
- **Correlation:** this is the weakest fit. It only picks up roughly linear relationships, one feature at a time, while kNN can find local patterns that correlation would miss. A low correlation wouldn't rule out predictive value.

One small refinement to your wording: k=1 is overfitting because each training point controls the area immediately around it, so the boundary follows noise. The jaggedness is a symptom that suggests overfitting, and comparing training and cross-validated scores in Part 2 is how you'd confirm it.

"""
Olivia Buchanan
Homework 4: kNN, Cross-validation, and PCA
"""

import spotifysongs
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Patch
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold, GridSearchCV
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.inspection import DecisionBoundaryDisplay

###################################################################################
# CONSTANTS
###################################################################################

# Seed
SEED = 17
np.random.seed(SEED)

# Load all tables as their own variable
globals().update(spotifysongs.load())

# Cross validation settings
NUM_FOLDS = 5

# Targets
CAT_TARGET = "mode"
NUM_TARGET = "popularity"

# Extra info for graphs
LABEL = "title"

# Numeric features
NUM_FEATURES = [
    "tempo",
    "valence",
    "speechiness",
]

# Categorical features
TIME_SIGS = ["time_signature_3", "time_signature_4", "time_signature_5"]

# Models to evaluate
SCHEMAS = [
    {
        "name": "kNN_boundary",
        "num": NUM_FEATURES[:2],
        "passthrough": TIME_SIGS,
        "cat": [],
    }
]

###################################################################################
# FUNCTIONS
###################################################################################

def build_pipeline(num: list,
                   cat: list,
                   passthrough: list,
                   k: int = None,
                   ) -> Pipeline:
    """
    Build a pipeline given the numerical and categorical features.

    Parameters:
        num (list): numeric feature names.
        cat (list): categorical feature names.
        passthrough (list): features to leave as-is.
        k (int): number of neighbors.

    Returns:
        Pipeline.
    """

    # Create feature transformers
    transformers = []
    if num:
        transformers.append(("num", StandardScaler(), num))
    if cat:
        transformers.append(("cat", OneHotEncoder(sparse_output=False,
                                                  handle_unknown="ignore",
                                                  drop="first"),
                                                  cat,
                                                  ))
    if passthrough:
        transformers.append(("pass", "passthrough", passthrough))

    # Return Pipeline depending on if k was given
    if k:
        # Neighbors specified
        return Pipeline([
            ("prep", ColumnTransformer(transformers)),
            ("knn", KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k)),
        ])
    else:
        # No neighbors specified
        return Pipeline([
            ("prep", ColumnTransformer(transformers)),
            ("knn", KNeighborsClassifier()),
        ])     

def evaluate_gridsearch_cv(model_schema: dict,
                           target: pd.Series,
                           train: pd.DataFrame,
                           k_values: list,
                           ) -> dict:
    """
    Evaluate logistic regression of a model.

    Parameters:
        model_schema (dict): schema of model names and features.
        target (pd.Series): the target to predict.
        train (pd.DataFrame): the features for training.

    Returns:
        Dict. Returns model results as a dictionary.
    """

    # Create Pipeline object
    model_pipeline = build_pipeline(num=model_schema["num"],
                                    cat=model_schema["cat"],
                                    )

    # Get list of features
    features = model_schema["num"] + model_schema["cat"]

    # Do GridSearchCV on k_values
    cv_output = GridSearchCV(
            model_pipeline,
            param_grid={"knn__n_neighbors": k_values},
            cv=KFold(NUM_FOLDS, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED),
            scoring="accuracy",
            refit="accuracy",
            )

content.text:
**Use `build_pipeline` as is, and keep the scaler.** Removing it would bring back the problem where tempo dominates the distances.

Having the scaler in the pipeline is also what keeps your cross-validation honest. `GridSearchCV` refits the whole pipeline for each k and fold, so the scaler learns its mean and SD from the training folds only. If you scaled everything beforehand, each validation fold would influence that scaling, which is data leakage.

Leaving out `k` is fine too, since the grid overrides `n_neighbors` for every candidate.

## Must fix in Part 2
These come from reading [knn.py](homework4/knn.py:231), not running it.

1. **Line 243:** `model_pipeline` doesn't exist in Part 2. You named it `knn_pipeline` on line 237.
2. **Line 250:** `grid.fit()` needs your features and target.
3. **Lines 233–234:** `fit` takes a single features table, so splitting it into `num_df` and `pass_df` won't work. Your `ColumnTransformer` picks columns by name, so select all of `NUM_FEATURES` and `TIME_SIGS` from `songs` into one DataFrame and it will send each column to the right place.

## Cleanup
- **Line 247:** you can remove `refit="accuracy"`. The default already refits on the best k, and naming a metric is only needed when you score with several.
- **Lines 96–107:** the two branches differ by only one argument. You could give `k` a normal default of 5, which is scikit-learn's default, and have just one return.
- **Lines 109–149:** `evaluate_gridsearch_cv` is never called and would crash if it were. Delete it or fix it, but don't leave it in as is.
- **Lines 51–58:** `SCHEMAS` isn't used by Part 2 either, and its name `kNN_boundary` no longer fits now that it includes time signatures.

## Worth adding
- **`return_train_score=True`:** this lets you compare training and validation accuracy across k, which is how you'd confirm the overfitting at k=1 we talked about.
- **`n_jobs=-1`:** you're running 250 fits (50 k values × 5 folds) on about 36,000 songs, so using all your CPU cores may save some time.
- **A baseline:** compare `grid.best_score_` with the share of songs in the most common class. That tells you whether the best k actually beats always guessing the most common mode.

message.content: my concern was that settings in pipeline like n_neighbors would lock it in to 5 when I really wanna do a gridsearch on n_neighbors. Are you saying that GridSearch overrides any settings necessary?

content.text:
Yes, but only the settings you list in `param_grid`. For each candidate, `GridSearchCV` clones your pipeline and sets those parameters on the clone, so whatever `n_neighbors` you built it with gets replaced. Your original `knn_pipeline` isn't changed.

The key `"knn__n_neighbors"` tells it where to apply the value: the `knn` step in your pipeline, then that step's `n_neighbors` parameter.

Everything else stays as you built it, including the scaler and the other kNN settings like `weights`.

So building with k=5, k=10 or no k at all gives the same search results. To confirm the search is using your values, check `grid.best_params_` after fitting, or the `param_knn__n_neighbors` column in `grid.cv_results_`, which should list all 50 values of k.

message.content: when I try and graph those accuracies, I get a key error that "mean_test_accuracy" doesn't exist. What's wrong? Is it "mean_test_score"?

content.text:
Yes, it's `mean_test_score`. When `scoring` is a single string like `"accuracy"`, scikit-learn always uses the generic name `score` in `cv_results_`, whichever metric you chose.

The metric name only appears in the keys when you pass several metrics, such as `scoring=["accuracy", "neg_log_loss"]`. You'd then get `mean_test_accuracy` and `mean_test_neg_log_loss`, and `refit` would need to name one of them.

If you added `return_train_score=True`, the training column follows the same rule: `mean_train_score`.

To see every available key, print `grid.cv_results_.keys()`.

import spotifysongs
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Patch
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold, GridSearchCV
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.inspection import DecisionBoundaryDisplay

###################################################################################
# CONSTANTS
###################################################################################

# Seed
SEED = 17
np.random.seed(SEED)

# Load all tables as their own variable
globals().update(spotifysongs.load())

# Cross validation settings
NUM_FOLDS = 5

# Targets
CAT_TARGET = "mode"
NUM_TARGET = "popularity"

# Extra info for graphs
LABEL = "title"

# Numeric features
NUM_FEATURES = [
    "tempo",
    "valence",
    "speechiness",
]

# Categorical features
TIME_SIGS = ["time_signature_3", "time_signature_4", "time_signature_5"]

###################################################################################
# FUNCTIONS
###################################################################################

def build_pipeline(num: list,
                   cat: list,
                   passthrough: list,
                   k: int = 10,
                   ) -> Pipeline:
    """
    Build a pipeline given the numerical and categorical features.

    Parameters:
        num (list): numeric feature names.
        cat (list): categorical feature names.
        passthrough (list): features to leave as-is.
        k (int): number of neighbors.

    Returns:
        Pipeline.
    """

    # Create feature transformers
    transformers = []
    if num:
        transformers.append(("num", StandardScaler(), num))
    if cat:
        transformers.append(("cat", OneHotEncoder(sparse_output=False,
                                                  handle_unknown="ignore",
                                                  drop="first"),
                                                  cat,
                                                  ))
    if passthrough:
        transformers.append(("pass", "passthrough", passthrough))

    # Return Pipeline
    return Pipeline([
        ("prep", ColumnTransformer(transformers)),
        ("knn", KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k)),
    ])

###################################################################################
# PART 1: DRAW KNN DECISION BOUNDARIES
###################################################################################

#     # Axis title
#     axis_title = str(k_values[i]) + "-Nearest-Neighbors"
#     ax[i].set_title(axis_title)

# # Plot title and save
# fig.legend(handles=[
#         Patch(color=cmap(0.0), label="minor"),

#     ])

# fig.tight_layout(h_pad=2)
# fig.savefig("decision_boundaries.png")
# plt.close(fig)

# print()

###################################################################################
# PART 2: FIND GOOD K-VALUE

print()
print("=" * 10, "PART 2: FIND GOOD K-VALUE", "=" * 10)
print()

# Split target from features
cat_target = songs[CAT_TARGET]
features_df = songs[NUM_FEATURES + TIME_SIGS]

# Get k-values
k_values = range(1, 76)

# Get pipeline
knn_pipeline = build_pipeline(num=NUM_FEATURES,
                              cat=[],
                              passthrough=TIME_SIGS,
                              )

# Make GridSearchCV for exploring k-values

grid = GridSearchCV(
    knn_pipeline,
    param_grid={"knn__n_neighbors": k_values},
    cv=KFold(NUM_FOLDS, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED),
    scoring="accuracy",

# Numeric features
NUM_FEATURES = [
    "tempo",
    "valence",
    "speechiness",
]

# Categorical features
TIME_SIGS = ["time_signature_3", "time_signature_4", "time_signature_5"]

###################################################################################
# FUNCTIONS
###################################################################################

def build_pipeline(model_type: str,
                   num: list,
                   cat: list,
                   passthrough: list,
                   k: int = 10,
                   n_comp: int = 2,
                   ) -> Pipeline:
    """
    Build a pipeline given the numerical and categorical features.

    Parameters:
        model_type (str): knn or pca model.
        num (list): numeric feature names.
        cat (list): categorical feature names.
        passthrough (list): features to leave as-is.
        k (int): number of neighbors.
        n_comp (int): number of components.

    Returns:
        Pipeline.
    """

    # Create feature transformers
    transformers = []
    if num:
        transformers.append(("num", StandardScaler(), num))
    if cat:
        transformers.append(("cat", OneHotEncoder(sparse_output=False,
                                                  handle_unknown="ignore",
                                                  drop="first"),
                                                  cat,
                                                  ))
    if passthrough:
        transformers.append(("pass", "passthrough", passthrough))

    # Return Pipeline
    if model_type == "knn":
        return Pipeline([
            ("prep", ColumnTransformer(transformers)),
            ("knn", KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k)),
        ])
    elif model_type == "pca":
        return Pipeline([
            ("prep", ColumnTransformer(transformers)),
            ("pca", PCA(n_components=n_comp)),
        ])
    else:
        return None

content.text:
**Your code looks right, but your conclusion needs rethinking, especially the 95% claim.** I read the code without running it, and your printed numbers add up.

`np.cumsum` is correct. One small refinement: cumulative variance is a running total, so each line adds the components up to that point, and only the last line adds everything. That last line is 94.3%, not 95%.

## Rethink these

**1. "95% of the features explain the target."** Both "features" and "target" are off here.
- Look at line 255, where you fit the PCA. What did you pass in, and is your target there?
- With that in mind, 94.3% of *what* is being explained? Try finishing this sentence: "Three components capture 94.3% of the ___ in ___."

**2. "Time signature may not be useful."** There are two questions to consider.
- If PCA never sees the target, can a small loading tell you whether a feature helps predict something?
- Your numeric features were scaled to variance 1, but time signatures weren't scaled. Estimate the variance of a 0/1 column using p(1 − p), with `time_signature_4` at p ≈ 0.90. How does that compare with 1? PCA looks for variance, so what would you expect it to do with those columns?

**3. "It slowly trickles down."** PCA always sorts components from most variance to least, so PC1 being largest isn't a finding. The size of the gaps is more informative.
- Your three values are 0.34, 0.32 and 0.28. What would it mean if PC1 were 0.80 instead?
- What does a nearly even split suggest about how correlated tempo, valence and speechiness are?
- Now add up the variances of all six columns, using your answer from #2. What share of that total comes from the three numeric features, and how does it compare with 94.3%?

## Refine these

Your reading of each PC is a good start, but you're leaving out some large loadings. Treat roughly 0.4 or more as worth mentioning, and consider the signs too.

- **PC1:** "upbeat" fits tempo and valence, but what does speechiness at −0.43 add?
- **PC2:** you only mentioned speechiness, but valence is 0.67, nearly as large. What kind of song scores high on both? Also, check how Spotify defines speechiness: does it measure singing or spoken words?
- **PC3:** this isn't just tempo. Which features move in the same direction, and which moves the opposite way? Each PC describes a contrast between features, so what kind of song would score high here, and what kind would score low?

A sign on its own doesn't mean anything, because flipping every sign in a component gives an equivalent result. What matters is which features share a sign and which have opposite signs.
